narrative:
The 2020 Boston Red Sox entered the pandemic-shortened 60-game season without ace Chris Sale and facing questions about a roster in transition. Those questions were answered quickly and painfully. A rough July start set the tone, and August brought only modest improvement as the bullpen repeatedly turned close games into losses. Aaron Judge's early crushing blow off Matt Barnes signaled what kind of year this would be for Boston's relief corps — a group that would become the defining weakness of a deeply flawed team.

The one bright spot came in August, when Mitch Moreland delivered a massive two-run homer that briefly suggested the offense could carry the club. September opened with some genuine hope — Xander Bogaerts went deep, Bobby Dalbec arrived and showed the kind of raw power that hinted at a brighter future, and the team finally strung together a winning month at 12-13. But the bullpen kept undermining every promising moment, with Josh Taylor and Phillips Valdez surrendering multi-run home runs at the worst possible times.

Matt Barnes emerged as a symbol of the season's frustrations, appearing in three of the campaign's most damaging moments — twice surrendering home runs and once presiding over a late-game collapse against Philadelphia that remains the single worst win probability swing of the year. The September finale against Atlanta was a microcosm of the whole season: the offense rallied with clutch hits from Rafael Devers and Kevin Plawecki, only for the bullpen to implode twice, with Freddie Freeman's two-run homer off Jeffrey Springs delivering the killing blow.

The 2020 Red Sox finished 24-36, last in the American League East, with the worst ERA among playoff contenders and a run differential of minus-59. Yet amid the wreckage were genuine reasons for optimism: Bogaerts remained an elite presence, Devers showed clutch instincts, and Dalbec's late-season arrival previewed a more powerful lineup to come. This was a lost season in every sense — compressed, chaotic, and ultimately a rebuilding year that Boston's front office would use as a catalyst for the remarkable turnaround that followed.

chapters.title: Out of the Gate Stumbling
chapters.description: Boston limps through July and into early August, with Aaron Judge's crusher off Matt Barnes setting a grim early tone.

chapters.title: Moreland's Moment of Hope
chapters.description: Mitch Moreland's go-ahead two-run blast in August sparks a winning month and hints that the offense can carry this team.

chapters.title: Bullpen Keeps Giving It Back
chapters.description: Late August sees the relief corps surrender critical multi-run home runs, erasing hard-won leads and stalling the team's momentum.

chapters.title: September Sparks and Collapses
chapters.description: The Red Sox flash genuine promise with Bogaerts and Dalbec going deep, but Matt Barnes and the bullpen deliver some of the most painful moments of the season.

chapters.title: Season Finale Heartbreak
chapters.description: Against Atlanta, clutch hits from Devers and Plawecki ignite a late rally only for Jeffrey Springs and the battered bullpen to surrender it all, closing the book on a lost season.
